screens.title: Data Transformation with $group and Accumulators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will master the $group stage and the set of accumulator operators that let you summarize collections. You will learn how the grouping key, defined in the _id field, determines which documents belong together, and how accumulators such as $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $push and $addToSet compute results for each group. We will ground the ideas with concrete examples drawn from sales and orders data: calculating total quantity by category, average price per category, and collecting item lists per group. You will also see common pitfalls — for example, accidentally grouping by _id and producing one group per document, or forgetting to use an accumulator to include a field in the output. By the end you'll be able to design a $group stage that produces counts, totals, arrays of values, or distinct sets, and combine $group with filtering and sorting to build real analytic summaries. Think about a report you might need to produce and how grouping would collect the necessary numbers and lists.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Data Transformation
Data Transformation with $group and Accumulators
Group documents with a grouping key and reduce each set with accumulator operators to produce analytics or collected arrays.
In this lesson

Grouping converts raw documents into actionable summaries for reporting, analytics, and dashboards.

screens.title: What the $group stage does
screens.narratorSegment: The $group stage groups input documents into buckets defined by an _id expression and then reduces each bucket to one document using accumulator expressions. A helpful analogy is sorting shopping receipts into labeled bins, where each bin holds receipts for one category and you then compute totals for each bin. In MongoDB the _id inside $group is that label expression: use a field like $category to group by category, or use null to combine everything into a single group. For example, grouping the sales collection by category produces a group for 'Electronics' and a group for 'Furniture'. Within each group you might apply $sum to total quantities and $avg to compute average price. A common misconception is to treat $group like a projection — fields not defined in _id or as accumulators will not appear in results. Another pitfall is accidentally grouping by the document _id, which isolates every document into its own group. As a takeaway, always plan your grouping key first and list the accumulator results you need. How would you label bins for your own reports? What the $group stage does means $group partitions documents by _id and computes accumulator results per partition; plan _id to match your reporting needs.. In practical terms, definition, analogy, and a sales example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What $group does
Definition & Analogy
Group partitions documents using an _id expression and reduces each partition with accumulator operators, like sorting receipts into bins and summarizing each bin.
Plan the _id
Choose a field or expression that matches the grouping you need, for example $category.
What appears in output
Only the _id and explicitly defined accumulators will be present in each output document.
Key Takeaway

Treat $group as a partition + reduce step. Misdefining _id is the most common cause of wrong aggregation results.

Concrete example — sales by category
Given a sales collection, grouping by $category then applying $sum and $avg produces per-category summaries.
{
  "$group": {
    "_id": "$category",
    "totalQuantitySold": { "$sum": "$quantity" },
    "averagePrice": { "$avg": "$price" },
    "numberOfSales": { "$sum": 1 }
  }
}
Misconception
You cannot reference unspecified fields in the output unless they are part of _id or defined via an accumulator.
Question
If you set _id: null what will your output show? (Hint: one group for the whole dataset)

screens.title: Numeric accumulators: $sum, $avg, $min, $max
screens.narratorSegment: Numeric accumulators give you the basic statistical building blocks inside a $group stage. Use $sum to compute totals over a numeric expression; pass 1 to $sum when you need a count of documents per group. Use $avg to compute the arithmetic mean across values in a group. $min and $max return the smallest or largest value present in the group, which is useful for ranges or boundary checks. For example with sales data you might use $sum on quantity to get total units sold, $avg on price to get the average sale price, and $min/$max on date or price to find earliest or largest values. A common mistake is expecting $avg to ignore nulls or missing fields — accumulators operate only over values present in the input documents; missing fields change the effective sample. Another nuance is numeric types: if fields are inconsistent between integers and decimals you can still compute aggregates, but be mindful of precision when interpreting averages. Practice by writing a $group that produces totalQuantitySold, averagePrice, minPrice, and maxPrice for each category. Numeric accumulators: $sum, $avg, $min, $max means $sum totals or counts, $avg measures central tendency, and $min/$max find extremes — choose based on the statistic you need.. In practical terms, when and how to use each numeric accumulator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Numeric Accumulators
Accumulator quick reference
$sum
Sum numeric values, or use $sum:1 to count documents in a group.
$avg
Compute the average of numeric values present in each group.
$min / $max
Return minimum or maximum values, useful for boundaries and ranges.
Common pitfall: missing or null fields affect $avg and $sum behavior. Confirm your input documents contain the fields you aggregate.
Example aggregation
Compute totals, average, and extremes per category.
{
  "$group": {
    "_id": "$category",
    "totalQuantitySold": { "$sum": "$quantity" },
    "averagePrice": { "$avg": "$price" },
    "minPrice": { "$min": "$price" },
    "maxPrice": { "$max": "$price" }
  }
}
Concrete result
Electronics: totalQuantitySold 4, averagePrice 433.33, minPrice 25, maxPrice 1200.
Misconception
Using $avg on string fields will not compute numbers; ensure types are numeric before aggregating.

screens.title: $first and $last: ordering matters
screens.narratorSegment: The $first and $last accumulators return values from the first or last document within each group as defined by the input order to $group. Because $group itself is unordered, you usually place a $sort stage before $group when you rely on these accumulators. For example, if you want the earliest sale per category, sort by date ascending and then group by category, using $first to capture that earliest date or associated item. A concrete example: with sales documents that include a date field, add { $sort: { date: 1 } } before your $group. A common mistake is expecting $first to return the first document in the original collection order; aggregation order matters and you must explicitly sort the stream feeding $group. Another nuance: large sorts can be expensive; if you only need the min or max value consider $min/$max on the field instead of sorting unless you require additional fields tied to that document. As a takeaway, choose $first/$last when you need an entire field from an ordered selection and use $min/$max when you only need the boundary value.

keyIdea.title: Ordering nuance
keyIdea.text: Use $sort before $group to make $first and $last deterministic; otherwise use $min/$max for boundary values without sorting.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › $first & $last
Process example
Sort the stream before grouping when $first or $last must reflect a specific order.
db.sales.aggregate([
  { $sort: { date: 1 } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$category",
      firstSaleDate: { $first: "$date" },
      firstItem: { $first: "$item" }
    }
  }
])
When to sort
Sort when you need a document-level field tied to an ordered selection.
Alternative
If only the smallest or largest value is needed, use $min or $max to avoid expensive sorts.
Concrete example

Find the earliest sale item per category by sorting ascending on date then using $first on item and date.

Pitfall

Relying on natural insertion order without sorting can lead to nondeterministic $first/$last results.

Check

Ask: do I need a full document field from the ordered row, or just a boundary value? Choose $first/$last or $min/$max accordingly.

screens.title: $push vs $addToSet
screens.narratorSegment: There are two primary ways to collect values into arrays inside $group: $push and $addToSet. $push appends every computed value for each document in the group, preserving duplicates and order. $addToSet adds values only if they are not already present in the group's array, effectively producing a unique list. Use $push when you need a full chronological or repeated record of values, for example compiling each action a user took. Use $addToSet when you only care about distinct elements, such as a list of unique tags. A concrete example from the sales collection: itemsSold: { $push: "$item" } produces an array of all sold items, including duplicates, while distinctItemsSold: { $addToSet: "$item" } produces unique item names. A common misconception is that $addToSet preserves order; it does not guarantee order. If you need both uniqueness and a predictable order, you may need to $addToSet first and then $unwind and $sort in a subsequent pipeline, or sort after grouping. As a takeaway, pick $push for full lists and $addToSet for uniqueness and consider additional stages when order matters for sets. $push vs $addToSet means $push retains duplicates and order; $addtoset produces unique arrays. choose based on whether duplicates matter and whether you need ordering guarantees.. In practical terms, collecting lists and ensuring uniqueness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › $push vs $addToSet
Two collection strategies
$push
Collects every value into an array. Duplicates remain and relative order is preserved based on input order.
$addToSet
Adds values only if not present, producing unique arrays. Order is not guaranteed.
{
  "itemsSold": { "$push": "$item" },
  "distinctItemsSold": { "$addToSet": "$item" }
}
Concrete example

Electronics itemsSold could be ["Laptop","Mouse","Keyboard"], while distinctItemsSold will list unique names; duplicates would be removed.

Misconception

addToSet is not a stable ordered set. If you require sorted unique values, apply additional stages after grouping.

Pro tip

If you need deduplication and ordering, consider $addToSet then $project with $size or a later $unwind + $sort step.

screens.title: Combining $group with other stages
screens.narratorSegment: Aggregation pipelines are sequences of stages that transform a stream of documents. A common architecture is to filter early with $match, shape or compute derived fields with $project or $addFields, then apply $group to summarize, and finally $sort or $project the aggregated output. Filtering first reduces work for grouping. Shaping inputs ensures accumulators receive the fields they expect: for example, compute a subtotal as quantity times price before grouping if you want to sum totals per order. A concrete pattern: use $project to create subtotal, use $group to sum subtotal by orderId and to collect productIds with $addToSet, then use a final $project to rename or compute counts from arrays. Common mistakes include grouping before shaping, which can make fields unavailable for accumulators, or forgetting to remove unnecessary fields that increase memory use. As a takeaway, design your pipeline by asking: what fields must exist at $group time, and which stages reduce volume beforehand? This approach keeps aggregations efficient and correct. Combining $group with other stages means filter early, compute fields next, then group. shape inputs so accumulators operate on the intended values and volume is reduced.. In practical terms, filter, shape, group, then sort — a repeatable sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Pipeline Architecture
Repeatable pipeline pattern
Filter first, compute derived fields, group to aggregate, then sort or reshape results.
Stage 1: $match
Reduce document set early to save work for $group.
Stage 2: $project / $addFields
Compute derived values like subtotal before grouping.
Stage 3: $group
Aggregate per key using accumulators on shaped inputs.
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $project: { orderId: 1, productId: 1, subtotal: { $multiply: ["$quantity", "$price"] } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$orderId",
      totalRevenue: { $sum: "$subtotal" },
      distinctProducts: { $addToSet: "$productId" }
    }
  }
])
Concrete benefit
Computing subtotal first yields correct totals without repeating arithmetic inside each accumulator.
Common mistake
Putting $group before the projection can make subtotal unavailable to $sum.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Orders Example
Starter data
Each document is an order line with orderId, productId, quantity, and price. Compute subtotal before grouping.
// Project subtotal then group by orderId
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $project: { orderId: 1, productId: 1, subtotal: { $multiply: ["$quantity", "$price"] } } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$orderId",
      totalRevenue: { $sum: "$subtotal" },
      distinctProductIds: { $addToSet: "$productId" }
    }
  }
])
Concrete result
For ORD001 totalRevenue sums subtotals from two lines for PROD001 and one for PROD002, while distinctProductIds lists PROD001 and PROD002 once each.
Misconception

distinctProductIds is an array, not a count. Use $size in a following stage to compute the number of distinct products.

Try this

To get a distinct product count, add a following $project: { distinctCount: { $size: "$distinctProductIds" } }.

Compute per-document values first, then aggregate; verify arrays vs counts with subsequent stages.

screens.title: Troubleshooting _id and missing fields
screens.narratorSegment: Two common sources of incorrect aggregation results are misdefining the _id grouping key and expecting fields that were never produced for the group. If you mistakenly use _id: "$_id" inside $group you will end up with one group per document because each document has a unique identifier. Conversely, using _id: {} or null groups everything into a single bucket, which may be correct for dataset-wide totals but wrong for per-key summaries. Another frequent issue is referencing a field in the $group output without defining it as part of _id or an accumulator. Since $group emits only _id and accumulator fields, such references simply won't appear. To detect these problems, run partial pipelines on a small sample, inspect intermediate outputs by inserting a $project stage before $group, and add a final $project to compute derived counts from arrays if needed. As a practical check, ask whether each output field is computed by an accumulator or is present inside the _id expression. This question quickly reveals missing definitions. screens.title: Designing complex summarizations
screens.narratorSegment: Complex summaries often require hierarchical grouping or multiple reduction steps. You can group by a composite key, such as an object containing multiple fields, to create multi-dimensional summaries. For example _id: { category: "$category", month: { $month: "$date" } } creates groups by category and month. Another pattern is staged aggregation: group to compute mid-level summaries, then unwind or reshape and group again to compute higher-level statistics. For the sales example you might first group by category and item to compute per-item totals, then group those results by category to compute category aggregates like top-selling item. A concrete approach: use an initial $group that computes item-level totals, project the results into a reduced shape, and then apply a second $group to compute category totals and pick the item with the highest total. A common misconception is that deeply nested grouping is always slower; thoughtful use of projection and limiting intermediate fields can keep memory use low. As a takeaway, think of grouping as a composable set of reductions that can be stacked to produce multi-level analytics. screens.title: Performance and memory considerations
screens.narratorSegment: When designing $group stages pay attention to performance and memory use. Grouping can be memory-intensive because groups are held in memory by the aggregation engine while accumulators process inputs. Reduce the volume and width of documents before grouping: use $match to filter irrelevant documents, $project to remove unneeded fields, and compute only the derived values the group needs. If grouping by high-cardinality fields creates too many groups, reassess whether you need that granularity or whether a downstream rollup makes sense. Also choose accumulators that avoid unnecessary overhead: prefer $sum and numeric accumulators over building large arrays with $push unless you truly need the full list. For distinct lists, $addToSet reduces duplicates but can still grow large; consider storing precomputed keys or sampling if arrays become huge. Finally, monitor your query plan and test pipelines on representative data; small-sample checks catch logic errors while larger tests reveal memory and performance behavior. The central rule is to shape and reduce data before grouping so accumulators run on compact, relevant inputs. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will master the $group stage and the set of accumulator operators that let you summarize collections. You will learn how the grouping key, defined in the _id field, determines which documents belong together, and how accumulators such as $sum, $avg, $min, $max, $push and $addToSet compute results for each group. We will ground the ideas with concrete examples drawn from sales and orders data: calculating total quantity by category, average price per category, and collecting item lists per group. You will also see common pitfalls — for example, accidentally grouping by _id and producing one group per document, or forgetting to use an accumulator to include a field in the output. By the end you'll be able to design a $group stage that produces counts, totals, arrays of values, or distinct sets, and combine $group with filtering and sorting to build real analytic summaries. Think about a report you might need to produce and how grouping would collect the necessary numbers and lists.

By the end of this chapter you will understand why $group exists and how it maps to common analytical needs. You will be able to choose an _id expression that defines groups correctly, avoiding grouping that is too fine or too coarse. You will know how to use numeric accumulators like $sum, $avg, $min, and $max to calculate totals and statistics, including using $sum with an argument of one to count documents. You will also be able to collect values into arrays using $push and to gather distinct values with $addToSet, and you will understand when each is appropriate. Finally, you'll learn to combine $group with filtering and sorting stages to create robust aggregation pipelines and to identify typical mistakes when _id is misdefined. Each objective emphasizes practical examples such as sales per category and order-level revenue so you can apply these skills right away.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills and checks you will use while building aggregation pipelines. First, you will practice using $sum with 1 to count documents and with a field to total numeric values, a pattern that appears frequently in reports. Second, you will learn to collect values into arrays, choosing $push when you need full lists and $addToSet when you only want distinct entries. Third, you will practice sequencing pipeline stages: filter with $match, shape with $project or $addFields, then group, and optionally sort the aggregated results. Fourth, you will run quick troubleshooting checks: verify your _id expression, confirm fields referenced in accumulators exist in inputs, and ensure ordering matters when using $first or $last. Each objective includes a concrete exercise or check so you can validate competency with real sample data like sales or orders.

The $group stage groups input documents into buckets defined by an _id expression and then reduces each bucket to one document using accumulator expressions. A helpful analogy is sorting shopping receipts into labeled bins, where each bin holds receipts for one category and you then compute totals for each bin. In MongoDB the _id inside $group is that label expression: use a field like $category to group by category, or use null to combine everything into a single group. For example, grouping the sales collection by category produces a group for 'Electronics' and a group for 'Furniture'. Within each group you might apply $sum to total quantities and $avg to compute average price. A common misconception is to treat $group like a projection — fields not defined in _id or as accumulators will not appear in results. Another pitfall is accidentally grouping by the document _id, which isolates every document into its own group. As a takeaway, always plan your grouping key first and list the accumulator results you need. How would you label bins for your own reports? What the $group stage does means $group partitions documents by _id and computes accumulator results per partition; plan _id to match your reporting needs.. In practical terms, definition, analogy, and a sales example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Numeric accumulators give you the basic statistical building blocks inside a $group stage. Use $sum to compute totals over a numeric expression; pass 1 to $sum when you need a count of documents per group. Use $avg to compute the arithmetic mean across values in a group. $min and $max return the smallest or largest value present in the group, which is useful for ranges or boundary checks. For example with sales data you might use $sum on quantity to get total units sold, $avg on price to get the average sale price, and $min/$max on date or price to find earliest or largest values. A common mistake is expecting $avg to ignore nulls or missing fields — accumulators operate only over values present in the input documents; missing fields change the effective sample. Another nuance is numeric types: if fields are inconsistent between integers and decimals you can still compute aggregates, but be mindful of precision when interpreting averages. Practice by writing a $group that produces totalQuantitySold, averagePrice, minPrice, and maxPrice for each category. Numeric accumulators: $sum, $avg, $min, $max means $sum totals or counts, $avg measures central tendency, and $min/$max find extremes — choose based on the statistic you need.. In practical terms, when and how to use each numeric accumulator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The $first and $last accumulators return values from the first or last document within each group as defined by the input order to $group. Because $group itself is unordered, you usually place a $sort stage before $group when you rely on these accumulators. For example, if you want the earliest sale per category, sort by date ascending and then group by category, using $first to capture that earliest date or associated item. A concrete example: with sales documents that include a date field, add { $sort: { date: 1 } } before your $group. A common mistake is expecting $first to return the first document in the original collection order; aggregation order matters and you must explicitly sort the stream feeding $group. Another nuance: large sorts can be expensive; if you only need the min or max value consider $min/$max on the field instead of sorting unless you require additional fields tied to that document. As a takeaway, choose $first/$last when you need an entire field from an ordered selection and use $min/$max when you only need the boundary value.

There are two primary ways to collect values into arrays inside $group: $push and $addToSet. $push appends every computed value for each document in the group, preserving duplicates and order. $addToSet adds values only if they are not already present in the group's array, effectively producing a unique list. Use $push when you need a full chronological or repeated record of values, for example compiling each action a user took. Use $addToSet when you only care about distinct elements, such as a list of unique tags. A concrete example from the sales collection: itemsSold: { $push: "$item" } produces an array of all sold items, including duplicates, while distinctItemsSold: { $addToSet: "$item" } produces unique item names. A common misconception is that $addToSet preserves order; it does not guarantee order. If you need both uniqueness and a predictable order, you may need to $addToSet first and then $unwind and $sort in a subsequent pipeline, or sort after grouping. As a takeaway, pick $push for full lists and $addToSet for uniqueness and consider additional stages when order matters for sets. $push vs $addToSet means $push retains duplicates and order; $addtoset produces unique arrays. choose based on whether duplicates matter and whether you need ordering guarantees.. In practical terms, collecting lists and ensuring uniqueness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Aggregation pipelines are sequences of stages that transform a stream of documents. A common architecture is to filter early with $match, shape or compute derived fields with $project or $addFields, then apply $group to summarize, and finally $sort or $project the aggregated output. Filtering first reduces work for grouping. Shaping inputs ensures accumulators receive the fields they expect: for example, compute a subtotal as quantity times price before grouping if you want to sum totals per order. A concrete pattern: use $project to create subtotal, use $group to sum subtotal by orderId and to collect productIds with $addToSet, then use a final $project to rename or compute counts from arrays. Common mistakes include grouping before shaping, which can make fields unavailable for accumulators, or forgetting to remove unnecessary fields that increase memory use. As a takeaway, design your pipeline by asking: what fields must exist at $group time, and which stages reduce volume beforehand? This approach keeps aggregations efficient and correct. Combining $group with other stages means filter early, compute fields next, then group. shape inputs so accumulators operate on the intended values and volume is reduced.. When designing $group stages pay attention to performance and memory use. Grouping can be memory-intensive because groups are held in memory by the aggregation engine while accumulators process inputs. Reduce the volume and width of documents before grouping: use $match to filter irrelevant documents, $project to remove unneeded fields, and compute only the derived values the group needs. If grouping by high-cardinality fields creates too many groups, reassess whether you need that granularity or whether a downstream rollup makes sense. Also choose accumulators that avoid unnecessary overhead: prefer $sum and numeric accumulators over building large arrays with $push unless you truly need the full list. For distinct lists, $addToSet reduces duplicates but can still grow large; consider storing precomputed keys or sampling if arrays become huge. Finally, monitor your query plan and test pipelines on representative data; small-sample checks catch logic errors while larger tests reveal memory and performance behavior. The central rule is to shape and reduce data before grouping so accumulators run on compact, relevant inputs. Second, select the correct accumulators: numeric ones like $sum, $avg, $min, $max for statistics, and $first/$last when order is meaningful — which requires sorting before grouping.
